## Methodology

### Introduction

The **Sports Business Classroom Fantasy Basketball League (SBCFBL)** is a 30-team league founded in 2020 by Sports Business Classroom alumni. It is built to feel more like running an NBA front office than playing a standard fantasy game: every organization has its own identity, manages a deep roster, and competes within a structure inspired by NBA team building and the collective bargaining agreement.

This project asks a question that standings and raw totals cannot answer on their own: **how does a fantasy roster fit together?** Four related questions organize the analysis:

1. How valuable is a player in each scoring category and across the complete matchup?
2. How likely is a projected roster to defeat an average opponent?
3. Does that roster convert its category strength into matchup wins efficiently, or is value stranded in categories it is already punting?
4. Which players are statistically similar, and which roster destinations make the best use of their particular production?

<div class="method-pipeline"><div><span>01</span><strong>Frozen Sources</strong><small>Fantrax · projections · six seasons · NBA schedules</small></div><i>→</i><div><span>02</span><strong>Canonical Data</strong><small>IDs · totals · rates · attempts · roster status</small></div><i>→</i><div><span>03</span><strong>Win Models</strong><small>13 categories · one overall matchup model</small></div><i>→</i><div><span>04</span><strong>Roster Simulation</strong><small>skill · expected score · chemistry · player fit</small></div><i>→</i><div><span>05</span><strong>Player Identity</strong><small>archetypes · specialists · Ward neighbors</small></div></div>

### League Format and Scoring

SBCFBL contains 30 organizations across two conferences and six divisions. Each team plays a **72-game regular season across 36 periods**. A period lasts approximately three to four days, and every team plays **two games simultaneously** during that window.

Scoring is inspired by the United States Electoral College: each basketball category carries a different point value based on its importance to winning. A team earns that category's full weight by defeating its opponent in the category, producing a 413-point scoring system rather than a conventional one-category, one-point format.

```{python}
scoring = categories[["category", "weight"]].copy()
scoring["category"] = scoring["category"].replace({"ST": "STL", "TO": "TOV"})
scoring.loc[scoring["category"].eq("TOV"), "category"] = "TOV*"
scoring_table = scoring.set_index("category")["weight"].to_frame().T
scoring_table.index = ["Weight"]
scoring_table.columns.name = "Category"
display(scoring_table)
```

\* **TOV is lower-is-better.** Every other category is higher-is-better. The 13 category weights total **413**.

The unequal weights are central to every downstream output. A one-point increase in the chance of winning PTS is worth six times the same probability change in MP because PTS carries 60 electoral points and MP carries 10. Expected Score therefore stays in the league's natural 413-point language rather than treating all categories as interchangeable.

### Data Sources and Frozen Snapshots

Current rosters, player identities, roster status, eligibility, and league scheduling are loaded from **Fantrax**. Player forecasts come from an external projection provider and are normalized into a common schema, allowing the source website to change without redesigning the analysis. Building an original NBA projection system would be an interesting project by itself, but it would combine two distinct research problems; this project treats external projections as the starting expectation and concentrates on their meaning inside SBCFBL.

League-wide research uses a frozen, one-time snapshot from the sister SBC Streamlit project: six completed seasons of team-period statistics and matchup results, the SBCFBL period calendar, active-player NBA game counts, and the historical NBA schedule. The 2026–27 NBA schedule is also saved locally. Quarto reads processed files and **never refreshes a website while rendering**, so the same source files always produce the same report.

| Source Layer | Grain | Role In The Project |
|---|---:|---|
| Fantrax roster export | One player-roster record | Franchise, roster status, eligibility, stable player ID |
| Projection snapshot | One projected player | Games, minutes, counting totals, shooting makes and attempts |
| Historical team-period results | One team in one matchup | Category totals, opponent, category outcomes, matchup outcome |
| SBCFBL period calendar | One scoring period | Period dates and season structure |
| NBA schedule archive | One NBA game | Actual NBA-game volume inside each SBCFBL period |

### Canonical Player Data Pipeline

Raw files are preserved before cleaning. Player names are display labels, not join keys: projections are reconciled to stable Fantrax IDs using reviewed aliases, then checked for one-to-one matches. NBA team abbreviations are normalized to `PHX`, `CHA`, `SAS`, and `NOP`; `(N/A)` becomes empty. A player without a current NBA team remains visible for roster accounting, but all projection values are set to zero so stale production cannot influence team models.

The projection provider stores FG%, FT%, and 3PT% cells with percentage, makes, and attempts together. Those components are split into numeric fields. Two-point production is reconstructed rather than guessed:

$$2PM = FGM - 3PM \qquad 2PA = FGA - 3PA \qquad 2PT\% = 2PM / 2PA$$

True shooting is recalculated from the underlying volume:

$$TS\% = \frac{PTS}{2 \times (FGA + 0.44 \times FTA)}$$

Season totals remain the modeling source of truth. The roster board converts counting totals to per-game values for readability, while the model retains games, minutes, makes, attempts, and totals for additive roster simulation. Missing or undefined display values are blank rather than presented as false zeroes.

### Historical Matchup Construction

The modeling unit is a **team-matchup observation**. Every completed head-to-head matchup contributes two linked rows—one for each opponent—with binary targets for the overall result and for each category result. Tied category outcomes are excluded from that category's regression because neither team won it. The two rows are not independent, so standard errors are clustered by matchup ID.

NBA opportunity varies by calendar window. To compare a short period with a long one, each historical counting total is converted to a common **24.93-NBA-game environment**, the observed mean across the archived regular-season periods:

$$x_{24.93} = \frac{x_{observed}}{NBA\ games\ in\ period} \times 24.93$$

This adjustment does not claim that one fantasy roster played 24.93 player-games. It controls for how many NBA games were available league-wide during the scoring window, which makes category thresholds comparable across periods.

### Standalone Category-Win Models

One logistic regression is fit for each of the 13 categories. For the nine counting categories—MP, PTS, OREB, DREB, AST, STL, BLK, TOV, and +/-—the only predictor is the category total standardized to 24.93 NBA games. The target is whether the team won that category:

$$P(Y_c=1\mid x_c)=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\alpha_c+\beta_c x_c)$$

The coefficient describes direction and steepness; the 50% threshold solves $-\alpha_c/\beta_c$; the odds ratio describes the multiplicative change in win odds from one additional unit. TOV is intentionally reversed: more turnovers should produce a negative coefficient and an odds ratio below 1. Curves are accompanied by observed win rates in 12 equally populated bins so model shape and empirical calibration can be judged together.

### Shooting Categories and Points Gained

Raw percentages ignore volume. A player shooting 50% on two attempts should not move a roster like a player shooting 50% on 500 attempts. TS%, 2PT%, 3PT%, and FT% therefore use **points gained** relative to that season's attempt-weighted league average:

$$PG=(Player\% - League\ Average\%)\times Attempts$$

For 2PT%, 3PT%, and FT%, attempts are 2PA, 3PA, and FTA. TS% uses the scoring denominator $2\times(FGA+0.44\times FTA)$, turning the percentage gap into points scored above or below league-average true-shooting efficiency at the same volume. Player contributions can be added directly to form a team-period value, remain centered near zero league-wide, and distinguish high-volume efficiency from small-sample percentage spikes. Historical shooting points gained is also adjusted to the 24.93-game environment before fitting the four category models.

### Overall Matchup-Win Model

The overall logistic regression uses all 13 category inputs simultaneously. Each is first expressed in the common 24.93-game environment and then z-standardized using the historical training distribution. Standardization makes coefficient magnitude comparable even though the inputs use different units:

$$P(Win)=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}\left(\beta_0+\sum_{c=1}^{13}\beta_c z_c\right)$$

This model estimates **conditional** effects. A shooting coefficient can appear modest when TS%, 2PT%, and 3PT% overlap because it asks what that metric adds after holding the other 12 inputs fixed. That is different from the standalone curve, which asks how often a team wins one category given only its performance in that category. AUC measures ranking ability, Brier score measures probability accuracy, and calibration bins compare predicted probabilities with observed matchup win rates.

### Season-Based Backtesting

Reported out-of-sample performance uses **leave-one-season-out cross-validation**. For each year from 2021 through 2026, every model is refit on the other five seasons and evaluated only on the excluded year. This produces six unseen-season folds for each of the 13 standalone category models and the overall matchup model. Fold predictions are pooled only after every season has served as the holdout.

The transformation logic remains fixed inside each fold: counting totals use the 24.93-game standard, shooting inputs use season-relative points gained, and the overall model learns its feature means, standard deviations, and coefficients from the five training seasons only. The held-out result is never used to fit model coefficients or standardization parameters. Saved outputs include every out-of-sample probability, fold-level results, pooled metrics, and ten-bin calibration tables.

Four metrics answer different questions. AUC measures winner-versus-loser ranking and is insensitive to the chosen probability threshold. Brier score is mean squared probability error. Log loss penalizes confident mistakes more severely. Calibration error is the observation-weighted absolute difference between predicted and observed win rates across probability bands. Reporting all four avoids declaring success from a single favorable statistic.

### Player Category and Overall Ratings

Each player rating is a controlled replacement experiment on an average 15-player roster. One average roster slot represents $24.93\div15=\mathbf{1.662}$ NBA games. For a category, the model removes one-fifteenth of the historical 50% benchmark, adds 1.662 games of the player's projected contribution, and recalculates the category-win probability. Ovr repeats that replacement across all 13 inputs and sends the complete profile through the overall matchup model.

The raw output is a probability change, but the displayed rating is min-max standardized across all projected players:

$$Rating_i=10\times\frac{Impact_i-\min(Impact)}{\max(Impact)-\min(Impact)}$$

That choice deliberately spreads the scouting scale: the best projected player is 10.0 and the worst is 0.0. It is a **relative player scale**, not a claim that a 7.0 player independently has a 70% chance of winning. The underlying probability score is retained in the processed data. Minors receive portable ratings when projections exist, but they are excluded from team aggregation until promoted.

### Team Aggregation and Skill

Team profiles sum every projected player who is **not in the minors**. Active, reserve, and injured-list designations all count because SBCFBL lineups rarely require meaningful bench decisions; the analytical question is the strength of the full usable organization. Each roster is evaluated against an average projected opponent after the current 30-team pool is centered on the historical 50% benchmark.

**Skill Level** is the overall 13-input model's probability of winning that matchup. **Expected Score** is calculated independently by multiplying each standalone category-win probability by its official weight and summing the 13 results:

$$Expected\ Score=\sum_{c=1}^{13}P(Win\ Category_c)\times Weight_c$$

League Rank orders current franchises by Skill Level. The variable-width Category Win Profile uses the same standalone probabilities: bar height is the chance of winning the category, and bar width is the category's share of the 413-point system.

### Team Chemistry and Player Fit

Chemistry measures whether the *combination* of category strengths works better or worse than its parts. First, Expected Score is translated into a historically calibrated baseline matchup probability. The residual is:

$$Chemistry\ Residual=P_{overall\ model}(Win)-P_{score\ baseline}(Win)$$

A positive residual means the full pattern of strengths—often a coherent punt with concentrated advantages—wins more often than the category-by-category score alone would imply. A negative residual means production is distributed in a less efficient way. Team Chemistry converts that residual into a historical percentile and divides by ten. A 5.0 is historically typical; an 8.0 exceeds 80% of completed team-period profiles. Because the reference distribution is fixed history rather than this season's best and worst teams, all 30 current teams can score well simultaneously.

Player Chemistry is a counterfactual roster experiment. A current non-minor player is removed; an outside player or minor-leaguer is added. The change in chemistry residual is calculated for every one of the **405 × 30 = 12,150** player-team destinations, then expressed as a global 0–10 percentile. High chemistry means the player's useful contributions reinforce categories the destination is positioned to win and avoid wasting production in weak categories.

Recommendation **Fit** is intentionally team-specific rather than another talent leaderboard. Within each player's 30 destinations, the chemistry-impact rank receives 65% weight and the Skill-impact rank receives 35%:

$$Fit=10\times(0.65\times Rank_{chemistry}+0.35\times Rank_{skill})$$

Favorite and Least Favorite Teammate use a pairwise second difference:

$$Interaction(A,B)=C(A+B)-C(A)-C(B)+C(neither)$$

Subtracting both standalone effects isolates what is unique about the pair. “Favorite” is the best available interaction, but it can still be negative if every teammate duplicates the same strengths.

### Archetype Membership Scores

Archetypes are explanatory scores, not hard unsupervised clusters. Each projected player receives a 0–100 membership score for eight basketball identities. Season totals capture usable fantasy volume; category breadth measures how many ways a player helps; per-minute quality separates skill from opportunity; shooting, TOV, and +/- capture downside.

| Archetype | Statistical Idea | High Score Means |
|---|---|---|
| Do-It-All Superstar | Elite talent + breadth + strong floor + opportunity | Top-end value without meaningful category holes |
| Star To Build Around | Talent + six-to-eight-category breadth + peak skills | A franchise anchor just below the exclusive superstar tier |
| Role Player | Balanced middle talent + dependable opportunity + low downside | Stable production that fits many roster shapes |
| Specialist | Strong peaks + concentrated positive value | Two or three categories can materially swing a matchup |
| Minute Filler | High opportunity + ordinary rate quality | Accumulation is useful even when efficiency is not |
| Negative Player | Opportunity + shooting/TOV/+/- downside + low talent | Playing the player can actively damage weighted categories |
| Bench Warmer | Low opportunity + low rate value | Too little volume or quality to move a matchup |
| Sleeper | Low opportunity + strong rate quality + peaks | More value could emerge if minutes increase |

The highest eligible score becomes the primary archetype. A secondary is shown only when it is at least 60 and at least 86% of the primary score. Order matters, so `Specialist / Sleeper` is distinct from `Sleeper / Specialist`; eight single labels plus 56 ordered pairs create 64 theoretical core outcomes.

Do-It-All Superstar is an exclusive top tier, never a secondary label. The tier size is constrained to five through ten players based on projection-pool size—seven currently—and candidates need at least seven category ratings of 6.0 or better. The highest-Ovr qualifiers receive the label; everyone else is prevented from using it so Star To Build Around remains meaningfully distinct.

### Specialist K-Means Subtypes

Specialist is one of the eight interpretable membership scores, but a separate five-cluster K-means model describes the *kind* of specialization. Five domain inputs summarize shooting, scoring, playmaking, defense, and interior production. Each player's domain mean is removed before clustering, which strips away general talent level and makes the algorithm focus on shape. Training candidates have a Specialist score of at least 50; inputs are standardized; deterministic farthest-first initialization makes the result reproducible.

The five centroids are assigned one-to-one to Shooting, Scoring, Playmaking, Defensive, and Interior Specialist by maximizing the total centroid-to-domain match across every possible assignment. The subtype adds detail without changing the primary/secondary 64-state framework.

### Ward Hierarchical Similarity

Similarity is intentionally independent from the named archetypes. Its feature matrix includes all 13 category ratings, projected season totals for minutes and counting production, shooting-attempt volume, and per-36 counting production. Every input is standardized; category ratings receive full weight, per-36 features receive 75% weight, and raw totals receive 45% weight. This balances three different questions: what categories does the player help, how much projected production reaches a fantasy roster, and what does the player do when actually on the floor?

Ward agglomerative clustering starts with one player per branch, then repeatedly merges the pair that causes the smallest increase in within-branch variance. The tree is cut at 12 branches for navigation. Nearest statistical neighbors are selected from the same branch whenever at least three candidates exist, using Euclidean distance in the **full weighted feature space**.

The League Overview map uses principal component analysis to compress that feature space into two dimensions. PCA is display-only: dot proximity is a useful overview, but exact branches and neighbors still use all features. The axes are therefore labeled as statistical components, not as “offense,” “defense,” or player quality.

### How To Read The Scales

<div class="scale-guide"><article><strong>Probability</strong><span>0–100%. A direct model estimate of winning a category or matchup against the defined opponent.</span></article><article><strong>Expected Score</strong><span>0–413 points. Weighted sum of the 13 standalone category probabilities.</span></article><article><strong>Player Rating</strong><span>0.0–10.0. Relative min-max position in the current projected player pool.</span></article><article><strong>Chemistry</strong><span>0.0–10.0. Historical percentile of interaction beyond the category baseline.</span></article><article><strong>Percentage Points</strong><span>Absolute change in win probability. +2.0 pp means 50% becomes 52%, not 51%.</span></article><article><strong>Fit</strong><span>0.0–10.0. A player's relative destination rank, emphasizing chemistry over raw Skill impact.</span></article></div>
